name: Jaruára
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Dixon, R.M.W. 2004. The Jarawara Language of Southern Amazonia (OUP) — Jaruara is a Jarawara dialect; grammar covers stress. Not online-accessible from here

new_statements.quote: The stress rule operates in terms of moras, with a short vowel counting as one mora and a long vowel as two moras. Now in the related Banawá dialect, stress goes on syllables including the first, third, etc. moras from the beginning of the word, ignoring a word-initial V in a word with three or more moras (see Buller, Buller and Everett 1993); the Jamamadí dialect has a similar rule. It is likely that this was the stress rule at an earlier stage of Jarawara. However, Jarawara now has penultimate assignment – stress goes on syllables including the second, fourth, etc. moras from the end of the word.
new_statements.citation: Dixon, R. M. W. 2002. The eclectic morphology of Jarawara, and the status of word. In R. M. W. Dixon & Alexandra Y. Aikhenvald (eds.), Word: A cross-linguistic typology, 125-152. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511486241.006

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is counted in moras (short vowel = 1, long vowel = 2) from the right edge of the phonological word: the syllable containing the penultimate mora is stressed, and so is every second mora before it (2nd, 4th, 6th... from the end). In a word with an even number of moras this coincides with the Banawá/Jamamadí left-to-right count (hósi), in odd-mora words it differs (Jarawara kobája vs Banawá kóbajá). A final long vowel (two moras) therefore carries the stress. Everett 1995:330 states the same for 'Yarawara' as trochaic right-to-left with main stress on the penultimate syllable, and Vogel 2006:46 reports Dixon 2004 as putting primary accent on the penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Dixon 2002 does not use the terms primary/secondary: it assigns stress to every even-numbered mora from the end (2nd, 4th,...), so the pattern is alternating rightward-anchored; Everett 1995:330 calls the penultimate the 'acentuação principal'; Vogel 2006:46 reports Dixon 2004 as 'primary accent... on the penultimate'.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and CVCV-reduplications consist of two phonological words, each stressed on its own penultimate mora (báni:kasáko, kéte:ketébe), not as one unit (p.128). n.2: the older counting-from-the-left rule survives as an 'underlying stress cycle' that conditions many phonological rules but is not the surface stress. Vogel 2006:46: words pronounced in isolation seem to carry accent on the ultima, possibly a phrasal-intonation effect. Everett 1995:330: Vogel (p.c.) reports exceptions to the Dixon & Vogel underlying-count rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (minimum two moras; monosyllables have a long vowel); the rule applies within each phonological word, and a grammatical word (compound, reduplicated verb) can contain two. Vogel 2006 notes citation-form (isolation) pronunciation may show final accent from phrasal intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: jaru1257 is a Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' languoid for the retired ISO 639-3 code jap 'Jaruára' (the MPG PuRe record of Vogel 2003 still tags it 'jap - Jaruára'). All sources describe Jarawara, the dialect jara1276 of Madi/Jamamadí jama1261 [jaa]; Everett 1995 calls it 'Yarawara'. The other Madi dialects (Banawá bana1307, Jamamadí east2800) have a different, left-to-right stress count, so the statement is dialect-specific to Jarawara.

sources.citation: Vogel, Alan. 2006. Jarawara-English dictionary. 2006 online edition. Cuiabá: Sociedade Internacional de Lingüística (SIL). 262 pp.
sources.note: Introduction (grammar sketch) p.46: 'There are complications also with respect to accent. Dixon (2004) says that the primary accent of a word falls on the penultimate. When a word is pronounced in isolation, it seems that the accent is on the ultimate, but this may have to do with the rules of phrasal intonation.' p.24: the morphophoneme I is realised i/e according to an even/odd count of preceding moras (long vowels and diphthongs count two).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Madí language' (Jarawara language redirects to it), section 'Syllables and stress', citing Dixon 2004.
sources.note: Second-hand: 'In the Jarawara dialect, stress is assigned to every second mora counting from the end of the phonological word, beginning with the penultimate, e.g. /ˌkaraˈɸato/ tape recorder. Since long vowels bear two moras, they are always stressed: /ˌbatiˈriː/ priest.' Banawá counts from the beginning; Jamamadi may share the Banawá system.

sources.note: Sec. 3.6.2.2 Acentuação (Yarawara), p.330: 'A regra de acentuação no Yarawara é trocaica, como no Banawá, mas vai da direita para a esquerda... A acentuação principal recai sobre a penúltima sílaba, indicando que há um pé iâmbico, não iterativo, construído à margem direita da palavra'; plus a second left-to-right count ('acentuação subjacente', Dixon & Vogel in progress) that deletes ha-syllables and changes vowels in odd syllables, with exceptions per Vogel p.c. Extrametricality 'apparently as in Banawá'. Sec. 3.6.3.2 p.331: no study of Jamamadí stress yet.
